title: Use only approved AI tools
rule: Keep one list of the AI tools your organization has approved and what each one may be used for. A new tool goes on the list before anyone uses it for work, not after.
why: Tools nobody approved are tools nobody checked. You cannot protect information that flows into a service you do not know exists.
manual: A shared spreadsheet with four columns: tool, approved uses, who approved it, date. Review it every quarter and remove what nobody uses.
how_this_site_does_it: This site keeps a ledger of every outside service it holds a credential for. A test fails when code starts using a credential the ledger has never heard of.

title: Keep sensitive information out of AI tools
rule: Keep personal information, case details, health, financial or law-enforcement records out of any AI tool that is not approved for that kind of information.
why: What goes into a chat window may be stored, reviewed by the vendor or used to train a model. Once it is out, it is out.
manual: Add a column to your approved-tools list: which kinds of information each tool may see. When in doubt, remove names and identifying details first.
how_this_site_does_it: This site keeps personal details out of its public code by test: one test fails if contact details appear in the repository, and another fails if a public page imports the module that handles a client's records.

title: A person approves before AI-drafted work goes out
rule: Anything an AI drafted that will be published, sent to the public or sent to another agency is read and approved by a named person first.
why: AI output can be wrong, off-tone or confidently invented. The approval step is where a person takes responsibility for it.
manual: Pick one approver per channel. Nothing AI-drafted is sent until the approver replies "approved" in writing, and you keep that reply.
how_this_site_does_it: On this site a drafted social post can only reach "needs review", never "approved", without a person. Public-records requests are drafted by software but sent only after approval; automatic sending is off by default.

title: Check drafts against a written list of things you never publish
rule: Keep a short written list of topics and claims your organization never publishes. Check every AI-drafted piece against it before it goes out.
why: An AI does not know your organization's lines unless you write them down. A list turns judgment calls into a check anyone can run.
manual: Five to ten lines on one page. The approver in the previous rule checks each draft against it and says which lines were checked.
how_this_site_does_it: This site runs a pre-send check against its own list in its outbound paths; a newsletter issue that trips it never sends. The list itself is kept in the code and tested for consistency.

title: Keep public-facing AI output nonpartisan
rule: AI-assisted content that speaks for a public body stays neutral on elections (candidates, parties, ballot questions) and critiques systems rather than people.
why: Public bodies owe residents neutrality, and many are bound to it by law. An AI draft can slip a political frame in without anyone noticing.
manual: Add a nonpartisan line to your never-publish list, and have your approver check each draft for it.
how_this_site_does_it: This site's list includes a nonpartisan rule, and the same rule is written into the instructions for the AI that critiques drafts before a person sees them.

title: Say when AI is involved, and never fake a person
rule: Tell people when AI wrote, summarized or answered something they rely on. Never present an AI voice, image or message as a real person.
why: Trust in a public body or a nonprofit is the whole asset. Being caught passing AI off as a person spends it all at once.
manual: One standard sentence on AI-assisted material, for example "Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by staff." No AI voices or avatars that imply a real employee.
how_this_site_does_it: On this site a computer reading a page aloud is labeled as a device voice, and in its language course a test keeps a synthetic voice from standing in for a native speaker.

title: Check facts and sources before you rely on AI output
rule: Before AI output is used in a decision, a publication or a reply to the public, a person checks its facts against the original source.
why: AI tools produce fluent text that can be wrong. A citation you did not open is not a citation.
manual: Require a source link for every factual claim in AI-assisted work, and have the approver open at least the ones that matter.
how_this_site_does_it: This site's assistant attaches the sources it drew on to every answer, its civic assistant only cites approved official sites, and research figures are recomputed by test on every change.

title: Put a spending cap on paid AI
rule: Every paid AI service has a monthly budget, a warning before it is reached, and a stop when it is.
why: Usage-based billing has no natural ceiling. A runaway automation or a busy public tool can spend a month's budget in a day.
manual: Set the vendor's own billing limit and alert, name who receives the alert, and write down what gets switched off at the limit.
how_this_site_does_it: This site tracks model spend month to date against a ceiling, warns at 80 percent, and pauses non-essential AI work when the ceiling is reached.

title: Limit how much the public can use your AI tool
rule: A public AI tool has a per-person limit and a total budget, so one visitor cannot use it all or run up the bill.
why: Anything free and public will be used at volume, sometimes by scripts. Limits keep the tool available and the cost predictable.
manual: Use the limit settings your vendor offers, and set a separate, lower budget for the public tool than for staff use.
how_this_site_does_it: This site's public assistant allows each visitor a set number of questions per minute, with further caps per hour and per day, and pauses for anonymous visitors when the monthly budget is spent.

title: Keep keys and passwords in one secure store
rule: API keys and passwords for AI services live in one secure store. They are never pasted into documents, chat messages, AI prompts or shared screens.
why: A leaked key is a bill and a breach. Keys pasted into chats and prompts end up in logs and histories you do not control.
manual: Use a password manager with a shared vault for service keys. Rotate a key whenever someone who had it leaves.
how_this_site_does_it: This site's setup flows read a credential on the server and write it straight to the store, so it never passes through a browser, and an audit checks that every credential in use is accounted for.

title: Give AI tools the least access they need
rule: When an AI tool connects to email, files or other systems, grant only the permissions its approved use requires, and review them when the use changes.
why: An AI tool with broad access can read, send or delete far more than anyone intended, and a compromised account inherits all of it.
manual: Before approving a connection, write down which permissions it asks for and why each one is needed. Refuse any you cannot justify.
how_this_site_does_it: This site requests only the permissions a feature uses, and a test fails if a connection ever asks for the forbidden ones.

title: Keep an off switch anyone on duty can use
rule: Every automated AI process that sends, posts or acts on your behalf can be stopped quickly by a named person, without waiting for a developer.
why: When something goes wrong at night or on a weekend, the question is how fast it stops, not who built it.
manual: For each automation, write one line: how to pause it and who is allowed to. Test the off switch once before relying on it.
how_this_site_does_it: This site has one switch that silences every notification channel at once, each channel's starting state is a recorded owner decision, and automatic sending of records requests stays off unless someone turns it on.

title: Keep a record of what AI did
rule: Keep a simple record of which AI tool was used, for what and by whom, with the date, for anything that leaves the organization or informs a decision.
why: A records request or an audit will ask what happened. "Someone used a chatbot" is not an answer.
manual: Note the tool and the reviewer in the file or ticket where the work lives. For recurring automations, keep the vendor's usage log.
how_this_site_does_it: This site logs every paid AI call with what it was for and what it cost, and reads its monthly spend from that log.

title: Watch for automations that quietly stop working
rule: Check on a schedule that each AI automation is still running and still doing its job, not only that it has not reported an error.
why: The most expensive failure is the one nobody notices: a reminder that stops sending, a report that stops arriving.
manual: A monthly checklist: each automation, when it last ran, and whether its output arrived. Anything that did not gets a person assigned.
how_this_site_does_it: This site has a dashboard that classifies every scheduled job as fired, failing or silent, and a test keeps that list in step with the jobs that actually exist.

title: Name an owner and review this policy on a schedule
rule: One named person owns this policy. It is reviewed at least every six months and whenever you add a tool, a use or a kind of data.
why: AI tools change monthly. A policy nobody owns describes last year's tools.
manual: Put the owner's name and the next review date at the top of the policy, and put the review on a calendar.
how_this_site_does_it: This page carries its own review date, kept in the same file as the rules, so the date and the rules change together.
